I've been farming these 50 mu for five years now — not the most experienced in the village, but I've learned fast. My neighbor Lao Zhang has been doing cabbage-cabbage-cabbage for over twenty years, and I watch what he does closely. Middle school means I can read the fertilizer bags and understand what the extension agent says, but honestly, most of what I know comes from my own fields and from talking to guys like Lao Zhang.

My farm is 50 mu, which is a decent size for vegetables around here. With four people in the house, we have family labor, but 50 mu of cabbage is a lot of work — transplanting and harvest are peak times when I have to hire people. I have well irrigation, which costs me more in electricity than the guys who pull from the river, but at least I can pump whenever I need.

Three crops a year on the same land is tight, but it's what works. I use zhonggan56 hybrid seedlings — I buy them from the seedling factory because I don't have time or space to grow my own with this schedule. The spring cabbage usually gets the best price, but it's risky with the cold. Summer is the most reliable for yield, but the pests are terrible. Fall prices are lower, but at least the land is working all year.

For fertilizer, I put down about one bag of 15-15-15 compound per mu as basal before transplanting. Then I topdress twice with urea — once when the plants are in rosette stage and again when the heads start forming — about half a bag total per mu split between the two times. The extension guy said cabbage needs a lot of nitrogen, and last year when I did this, the yield was good. I also spread some organic manure as base — maybe 100 kg per mu — my cousin has a livestock farm and I get it cheap.

For irrigation, spring is drier so I irrigate four times, summer is hot so I need six times, and fall I can get by with four. Border irrigation is what my equipment handles. Pesticide-wise, I spray herbicide before transplanting and then insecticide as needed — cabbage worms and aphids are the main problems. Summer I spray more because the pests are worse.

The biggest tradeoff is labor versus cash. Hiring people for harvest costs me, but if I don't get the cabbage out of the field when it's ready, I lose money. So I hire 5–6 people at harvest for each crop, and my family handles the transplanting, weeding, and irrigation. I also watch my cash — fertilizer and hired labor are my biggest costs, and I need to keep some reserve for emergencies.
